title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether deterministic verification plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device-configuration translation. The confirmatory design used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), gpt-5-mini as the generator, and a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared-initial-candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task reused across arms) and allowed at most one bounded repair attempt per task. All planned episodes completed (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) with model_calls_used = 240 (shared-generation). Every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms (n11 = 240; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Two preregistration→execution deviations materially constrain inference and are explicitly disclosed: (1) the executed shared-generation semantics invalidated the preregistered power calculation that assumed independent per-condition generation, and (2) a prespecified schema-constrained baseline comparison (GVR vs schema-constrained) was not executed and no recorded rationale appears in the archive. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR produced no verifier-detectable benefit in this specific, artifact-grounded setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred to correct. We archive the authoritative artifacts and describe reproducible next steps to restore discordance potential and evaluate GVR under adversarial, independent-generation, and multi-model regimes.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→device-configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) can increase operational efficiency but introduces risk: stochastic generators may output syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect commands that violate network invariants (reachability, required workflows, or security predicates). Prior work therefore recommends interposing deterministic validators and iterative repair loops—commonly described as generate–verify–repair (GVR)—to detect and correct mechanically checkable defects before execution. Evidence from code- and infrastructure-generation domains shows GVR-style pipelines reduce surface-level and syntactic errors, but measurable benefits for domain-specific semantic invariants in NetOps remain unsettled and sensitive to evaluation semantics and verifier coverage.

We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to answer a focused operational question: under a frozen, archived design that used a single generator/prompt pairing and shared-initial-candidate generation semantics, does inserting a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop reduce verifier-detected semantic invariant violations relative to an unconstrained baseline? The study was preregistered (study_id: c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1; preregistration_sha256: eaedeae9aa302327e090d519a7a16f514d7fb79a472071aaf171f2f618c8ad4d) and executed under an archived adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) using gpt-5-mini. We report the artifact-backed execution, the degenerate confirmatory outcome, explicit preregistration→execution deviations, and operationally actionable recommendations.
sections.related_work: Three literatures ground this study. First, LLM hallucination and code-generation failure studies document frequent fabricated outputs and motivate validator-instrumented pipelines (surveys and empirical analyses summarized in the evidence synthesis; e.g., generate-and-verify and hallucination-taxonomy works). Second, generate–verify–repair and grammar/schema-constrained decoding methods demonstrably raise syntactic/executable rates and reduce surface hallucinations in code and domain-specific synthesis, but their semantic guarantees vis-à-vis domain invariants vary by verifier completeness and task scope. Third, NetOps literature emphasizes verifier-driven evaluation (reachability/policy invariants), intent-based translators, and human-in-the-loop governance for high-stakes changes. Compared to prior work, our run is preregistered, paired, and artifact-archived; it differs because the executed shared-generation semantics eliminated within-pair stochastic variation and therefore altered the inferential conditions under which GVR’s benefit can be observed. Nearest-work comparison (compact): (a) generate-and-verify case studies — show reduced syntactic failures but limited semantic scope; (b) intent-translation systems — emphasize verifier-integration but often lack preregistration; (c) benchmarks for NetOps synthesis — provide task structure but vary in oracle completeness. Our study contributes a fully archived paired execution and an explicit account of how generation semantics interact with confirmatory inference.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands: The preregistered primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (proportion difference in verifier-detected semantic-violation rate computed pairwise). Two prespecified primary comparisons were registered: (C vs A) GVR vs unconstrained generation and (C vs B) GVR vs schema-constrained decoding; Bonferroni correction across these two comparisons (family alpha = 0.05 → per-comparison alpha = 0.025) was specified. The analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) and all analysis rules were frozen prior to execution.

Design and frozen execution contract: Confirmatory sample N = 240 tasks (12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks each). Requested generator model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA-256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Crucial frozen semantics recorded pre-execution: generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 (bounded single repair attempt). Model call budget = 480; the adapter executed under shared-generation to reuse one initial candidate per task across arms. These archived choices deterministically shaped the experiment’s inferential power.

Task bank, oracle, and scoring: The supplied synthetic NetOps task bank encodes starting device states, intents, workflow constraints, and expected final states; the deterministic validator implements pybatfish-style checks returning structured diagnostics (violation_count, violations list, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). Scoring rule: full_intent_constraint_validation via deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). Representative per-task validator traces (validation_before/validation_after) are archived and authoritative for scoring decisions.

Execution controls and handling of failures: The preregistration specified exclusion and missingness rules (complete_pair_primary) and a conservative sensitivity plan treating infrastructure failures as violations. Technical restarts were permitted only for genuine infrastructure recovery and were logged; none affected scientific outcomes in the archived run. The complete execution manifest (execution_manifest) documents planned_episode_count = 480 and completed_episode_count = 480.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact-backed): The adapter completed all planned episodes (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480; failed_episode_count = 0). Because generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, model_calls_used = 240 (one shared generation per task reused across arms). For every task the shared initial candidate (shared-initial) was identical to both arm responses; repair_applied = false for every episode (no repair attempt was triggered because the validator accepted the initial candidate). Representative per-task scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json) and execution/responses/* confirm these facts.

Primary confirmatory outcomes: The registered analysis executor produced the contingency table: n11 = 240 (both arms accepted), n10 = 0 (guarded-only accepted), n01 = 0 (baseline-only accepted), n00 = 0 (both rejected). Summary rates: baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI (paired_bootstrap_percentile; bootstrap_resamples = 10000; bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) are archived and authoritative for these numbers.

Degeneracy and statistical interpretation: Zero discordant pairs render paired inference degenerate: there is no within-pair disagreement to estimate an effect of the intervention under the executed semantics. The observed exact-test p = 1.00 and the collapsed bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] are deterministic consequences of the contingency and of using the preregistered paired analysis executor. Importantly, the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation (restoring discordance potential); the executed shared-generation semantics invalidate that power analysis for the observed run. These facts are archived and explicitly reconciled in the analysis artifacts (deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Unexecuted prespecified comparison and procedural deviation: The preregistration listed two prespecified primary comparisons (C vs A and C vs B). The archived execution artifacts document only the paired experiment comparing the unconstrained baseline (A) with guarded GVR (C) under shared_initial_candidate semantics; the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed and no recorded rationale for its omission appears in the execution artifacts. We explicitly label this prespecified-but-unexecuted comparison as a procedural deviation that reduces the evidentiary scope of the present run.
sections.discussion:
Conservative interpretation: Under the executed shared-generation semantics and the supplied synthetic workload, bounded GVR produced no verifier-detectable benefit because the generator+prompting produced verifier-acceptable outputs for every task. Two non-exclusive artifact-supported mechanisms explain the outcome. (1) Task/verifier alignment: the synthetic tasks, generator prompting, and validator predicates together defined a distribution for which the generator produced acceptable candidates deterministically. (2) Sensitivity reduction due to shared-generation: reusing a single initial candidate across arms removes independent generator stochasticity and therefore removes the within-pair discordance GVR could exploit.

Implications for evaluation design: Demonstrating operational value of GVR requires evaluation semantics aligned with inferential assumptions. If GVR’s efficacy depends on correcting generator stochastic failures, then evaluations must (a) permit independent per-condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true), (b) include adversarial or golden-reference tasks that reliably induce verifier failures, and/or (c) test across multiple generator families and prompt variants. Our archive contains the deterministic task manifest, RNG seeds, and adapter configuration; toggling generation_semantics and rerunning with independent per-condition generation restores the preregistered design logic and validates power arguments.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the preregistration→execution mismatch: the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation, which the executed shared-generation semantics violated. Construct validity depends on verifier completeness: passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 certifies only the encoded invariants; operational harms outside those invariants remain possible. External validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, a single generator (gpt-5-mini), a single bounded repair budget (one attempt), and a single verifier implementation. Conclusion validity is limited because zero discordance precludes evidence for GVR efficacy in the executed semantics. These limitations are enumerated in the archived manifest and the published limitations list.

Operational recommendations (artifact-grounded, reproducible): (1) Re-execute the preregistered paired design with independent per-condition generation to restore discordance potential; the archived task manifest and RNG seeds enable reproducible reruns. (2) Inject adversarial or golden tasks (the preregistration planned 10% golden tasks) whose expected verifier outcome is known to validate verifier sensitivity. (3) Expand model scope beyond gpt-5-mini and vary prompts to measure robustness. (4) Allow larger or iterative repair budgets and record repair iteration distributions. (5) Broaden verifier coverage (additional semantic invariants or formal/SMT hybrids) to reduce oracle incompleteness risk. The evidence synthesis identifies the research gap G2 (stronger integration with formal verification) as a promising direction.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact-archived paired experiment evaluating a bounded GVR intervention on a synthetic intent→configuration NetOps task bank. Under the executed shared-initial-candidate semantics (one shared generation per task reused across arms), every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms (n11 = 240), producing a null paired estimate (0.0), exact McNemar p = 1.00, and paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR did not provide verifier-detectable value in this specific, artifact-grounded setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred to correct. Two preregistration/execution deviations reduce the run’s inferential reach: (1) shared-generation semantics invalidated the preregistered independent-generation power assumption, and (2) a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed and lacks a recorded rationale in the archive. We therefore do not generalize beyond the executed model, prompt, task bank, verifier, repair budget, or generation semantics. We publish the authoritative archived artifacts and recommend reproducible follow-ups—independent per-condition generation, adversarial/golden injections, multi-model runs, and expanded verifier coverage—to robustly assess GVR’s operational value in NetOps.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also removed per-arm stochastic variation and therefore reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
